title: Retrieval-augmented generation: the pipeline and its failures
summary: Build a RAG pipeline end to end on a toy corpus: chunk size and overlap, top-k and token budgets, context ordering, citation prompts, separate retrieval and generation metrics, and the seven failure points.
outcomes: Explain how RAG combines parametric and non-parametric memory and why re-indexing updates knowledge
Predict how chunk size, overlap and top-k change what reaches the prompt, and compute a token budget
Explain the lost-in-the-middle effect and order retrieved chunks to reduce it
Compute faithfulness, context precision, context recall and ALCE citation recall and precision
Diagnose a bad answer as one of the seven RAG failure points

lessons.title: Why an LLM needs a retriever: parametric vs non-parametric memory

blocks.md:
An LLM stores what it learned in its weights. Lewis et al. (2020) call this **parametric memory**. It has three problems for real applications: it is frozen at training time, it has never seen your private documents, and it cannot tell you *where* a fact came from, so you cannot check it.

**Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG)** adds a second, **non-parametric memory**: an index of text that is searched at query time. The retrieved passages are given to the generator as extra input, so the answer can be grounded in them and cite them.

blocks.title: The RAG pipeline: an offline index and an online query path

scenes.caption: Offline indexing: split every document into chunks, embed each chunk with the same model you will use for queries, and store the vectors in an index. This runs once, and again whenever documents change.
Online retrieval: the question is embedded and the index returns the k chunks whose vectors score highest against it. Nothing about the LLM is involved yet.
Generation: the prompt builder packs the question and the retrieved chunks into one prompt within a token budget, and the LLM writes an answer that cites the numbered chunks.
Two memories: knowledge in the LLM weights (parametric) and knowledge in the index (non-parametric). Swap or re-index the documents and the system knows new facts without any retraining.

blocks.md: The original RAG model (Lewis et al., 2020) used a **DPR** retriever: two BERT-base encoders, one for documents and one for queries, scoring a document $z$ for input $x$ by the inner product $d(z)^\top q(x)$. The index was the December 2018 Wikipedia dump split into disjoint **100-word chunks**, 21M in total, searched with FAISS using an HNSW approximation. The generator was BART-large (400M parameters), which received the input concatenated with each retrieved passage.

blocks.tex: p_{\text{RAG-Seq}}(y \mid x) \approx \sum_{z \in \text{top-}k(p_\eta(\cdot \mid x))} p_\eta(z \mid x) \prod_{i=1}^{N} p_\theta(y_i \mid x, z, y_{1:i-1})
blocks.caption: RAG-Sequence: retrieve the top k passages, score the whole answer under each passage, and weight by the retriever's probability for that passage.

blocks.md: Read the formula left to right: the retriever $p_\eta$ gives each of the top $k$ passages a probability, and the generator $p_\theta$ gives the answer a probability *given* that passage. Summing over passages treats the passage as a hidden variable. **RAG-Token** does the same sum per output token, so different tokens can lean on different passages. Lewis et al. used $k \in \{5, 10\}$ in training and kept the document encoder and index fixed, fine-tuning only the query encoder and BART.

Two companion papers set the pattern still used today. **DPR** (Karpukhin et al., 2020) showed a dense dual encoder beats Lucene BM25 by 9 to 19 points of top-20 passage retrieval accuracy (78.4% vs 59.1% on Natural Questions). **Fusion-in-Decoder** (Izacard and Grave, 2021) encodes each retrieved passage separately with the question and lets the decoder attend over all of them, so cost grows linearly with the number of passages; accuracy kept improving as they used more passages, up to 100.

Most systems built today keep the retrieve-then-generate shape but skip joint training: the generator is an off-the-shelf LLM, and the retrieved chunks are simply pasted into its prompt.

blocks.prompt: Lewis et al. built a second index from a December 2016 Wikipedia dump and asked their RAG model, trained with the December 2018 index, about 82 world leaders who had changed between 2016 and 2018. What happens when the index and the question come from different years?
blocks.reveal: With matching index and leaders, RAG answered 70% (2016) and 68% (2018) correctly. With mismatched pairs, accuracy fell to 12% (2018 index, 2016 leaders) and 4% (2016 index, 2018 leaders). The model's answers followed the **index**, not its weights. This is **index hot-swapping**: update knowledge by re-indexing instead of retraining.

blocks.md: RAG splits knowledge in two: the index decides **what facts are available**, the LLM decides **how they are read and phrased**. Every quality problem in this course is a failure of one of these two halves, or of the hand-off between them.

RAG is not always needed. Anthropic's Contextual Retrieval post notes that if a knowledge base is under about 200,000 tokens (about 500 pages), you can place all of it in the prompt, and prompt caching makes that cheaper. Retrieval earns its complexity when the corpus is larger than the context window or changes often.

blocks.question: A team fine-tunes an LLM on their product docs every quarter. Docs change weekly, and users need links to the source page. What does RAG give them that fine-tuning does not?
options: Higher fluency, because retrieved text improves the model's grammar
Fresh facts by re-indexing without retraining, and provenance because the answer can cite the retrieved chunk
Lower latency, because retrieval is always faster than generation
Nothing; fine-tuning and RAG update knowledge in the same way
blocks.explain: The index is non-parametric memory: changing it changes what the model can see, as the hot-swap experiment showed (68% vs 4% on 2018 leaders, with the 2018 vs the 2016 index). And because the evidence is an explicit chunk, the answer can point to it. Retrieval adds a step, so it does not lower latency.

blocks.question: In RAG-Sequence, what does the term $p_\eta(z \mid x)$ contribute?
options: The generator's probability of each answer token
The retriever's weight for passage z, so answers supported by higher-scoring passages count more
A penalty for long passages
The probability that the question is answerable
blocks.explain: The sum runs over the top k passages. Each term multiplies the retriever's probability for passage z by the generator's probability of the whole answer given z. The retriever acts as a soft selector over evidence.

lessons.title: Indexing: how chunk size and overlap decide what can be found

blocks.md:
We will follow one toy corpus through the whole course. It is the HR handbook of a made-up company, Northwind, with six short documents:

- **D1** Parental leave (44 words): 16 weeks for the primary caregiver, **6 weeks** for a secondary caregiver, must begin within 12 months, requests go to the **People team**, who approve them.
- **D2** Vacation (25): 20 days a year, 5 carry over, your manager must approve vacation requests.
- **D3** Sick leave (28). **D4** Expenses (19). **D5** Remote work (20).
- **D6** Benefits overview (24): lists parental leave, vacation and sick leave, details are on each policy page.

The question: *How long is parental leave for a secondary caregiver, and who approves the leave request?* The correct answer: 6 weeks, approved by the People team.

A **chunk** is the unit you embed, retrieve and paste into the prompt. **Chunk size** is its length; **overlap** is how many units consecutive chunks share. We compare two strategies:

- **Strategy A**: each whole document is one chunk (6 chunks).
- **Strategy B**: fixed windows of 12 words with 4 words of overlap (18 chunks).

Simplified model: our retriever is cosine similarity between word-count vectors after dropping stopwords and a trailing plural s. It stands in for an embedding model so every score can be checked by hand; a real embedding model would give different numbers but the same kinds of failure.

blocks.title: Where chunk boundaries fall in document D1

scenes.caption: D1, the parental leave policy, is 44 words in six sentences. The two facts our question needs are S4 (6 weeks for a secondary caregiver) and S6 (the People team approves).
Fixed 12-word windows with no overlap cut at words 12, 24 and 36. Three sentences are split; S6 is cut after Send leave, so its second half no longer says what is being requested.
With 4 words of overlap each window starts 8 words after the previous one, so D1 becomes 5 chunks instead of 4. D1.3 holds S4 whole and D1.5 holds S6 whole.
The cost: words 8 to 12, 16 to 20, 24 to 28 and 32 to 36 are stored and embedded twice. Across the whole corpus, overlap 4 gives 18 chunks instead of 16.

blocks.title: Strategy A: whole documents as chunks

scenes.caption: Six chunks, one per document, scored by our stand-in retriever. D1 wins clearly at 0.687 because it shares parental, leave, secondary, caregiver, request and approve with the question.

Top-3 is D1, D6 and D2. D6 is a generic benefits overview and D2 is the vacation policy, pulled in by approve and request. One D2 sentence says your manager must approve requests, which is true for vacation only.
Same retriever, 18 small chunks. Scores are closer together: short chunks match on a few words, so a single repeated phrase like parental leave moves a chunk a lot.
Top-3 is D1.1, D6.2 and D1.5. D1.5 has the People team fact. D1.3, the only chunk with 6 weeks, scores 0.385 and lands at rank 4, just outside the cut.

blocks.md:
This is the core tradeoff, stated in the LlamaIndex docs: a smaller chunk size makes each embedding more precise, while a larger chunk may be more general but can miss fine-grained details. LlamaIndex defaults to chunk size 1024 and overlap 20 (in tokens), with `similarity_top_k` 2, and its example that halves the chunk size to 512 doubles top-k to 4 so the same amount of text is retrieved.

Splitting on structure helps. LangChain's recommended generic splitter, `RecursiveCharacterTextSplitter`, tries the separators `"

"`, `"
"`, space, then empty string in order, keeping paragraphs, then sentences, then words together as long as the size limit allows.

Small chunks lose their context. D1.5 reads *or adoption. Send leave requests to the People team, who approve them.* It never says which leave. In a real handbook with ten leave policies it would match every leave question equally well. Bigger chunks keep context but dilute the embedding and spend more of the prompt.

Anthropic's **Contextual Retrieval** attacks that problem at indexing time. For each chunk, an LLM is given the whole document and the chunk and asked for a short context situating the chunk, usually 50 to 100 tokens. That text is prepended to the chunk before it is embedded and before the BM25 index is built. For D1.5 the context might be *From Northwind's parental leave policy*.

blocks.title: Contextual Retrieval: top-20 retrieval failure rate

scenes.caption: Anthropic measured 1 minus recall@20 averaged over several knowledge domains. Plain embeddings missed the relevant chunk in the top 20 for 5.7% of queries.
Prepending a 50 to 100 token, LLM-written context to each chunk before embedding cut failures by 35%, and combining it with a contextual BM25 index cut them by 49%.
Reranking the contextual results brought the reduction to 67%. These are Anthropic's own benchmarks; measure on your corpus before assuming the same gains.

blocks.question: You switch from 1024-token chunks to 256-token chunks and keep top-k at 2. What is the most likely new problem?
options: Each chunk's embedding becomes vaguer, so precision drops
The prompt overflows the context window
The LLM now sees a quarter as much text, so answers that span several sentences may lose a needed piece
Overlap stops working because it only applies to large chunks
blocks.explain: Smaller chunks give sharper embeddings, but 2 chunks of 256 tokens is 512 tokens of evidence instead of 2048. That is why the LlamaIndex example doubles top-k when it halves chunk size. Our toy shows the same thing: with 12-word chunks the 6 weeks chunk sits at rank 4.

blocks.question: Why did overlap 4 make the People team fact retrievable as one chunk in D1?
options: Overlap makes the embedding model weight the last words of a chunk higher
Overlap removes stopwords at chunk boundaries
Overlap guarantees every sentence is whole in exactly one chunk
With windows starting every 8 words, S6 (words 34 to 44) fits wholly inside the window covering words 32 to 44
blocks.explain: Overlap does not guarantee anything about sentences; it only shifts where windows start. Here the shifted window D1.5 happens to contain all of S6. A sentence longer than the stride can still be cut in every window, which is why structure-aware splitters exist.

lessons.title: Top-k, the token budget, and where chunks sit in the prompt

blocks.md: **Top-k** is how many of the highest-scoring chunks you take from the index. It is the main dial between missing evidence (k too small) and burying it in noise and cost (k too large). There is no universal value: Lewis et al. tuned k on dev data, LlamaIndex defaults to 2, and Anthropic found passing 20 chunks beat 10 or 5 in their tests, while noting that more information can distract the model.

blocks.prompt: In Strategy B with k = 3, the context is D1.1, D6.2 and D1.5. Can the LLM answer both halves of the question?
blocks.reveal: No. D1.5 gives the People team, but 6 weeks lives only in D1.3, which scored 0.385 and ranked 4th, behind the benefits overview D6.2 (0.527). Nothing the LLM does can recover a fact that is not in its context. Barnett et al. name this failure **Missed the Top Ranked Documents**.

blocks.md:
So raise k? The prompt has a hard limit, and a toy one makes the arithmetic visible. Take a 128-word window. The instructions take 29 words, the question 15, and we reserve 24 for the answer. That leaves 60 words for retrieved text. Fill it in rank order and stop at the first chunk that does not fit:

- **Strategy A**: D1 (44 words) fits; adding D6 (24) would make 68 > 60. Context = D1 only.
- **Strategy B**: five 12-word chunks fill exactly 60: D1.1, D6.2, D1.5, D1.3, D1.2. Both facts are now in.

blocks.caption: Budget in tokens, not in chunks: the same 60 holds one whole document or five small windows.

scenes.caption: Fixed costs are 29 instruction words, 15 question words and a 24-word answer reserve, 68 in all. Each chunk adds c. With c = 12, k = 5 lands exactly on the 128-word window.
With chunks the size of D1 (44 words), only one fits: k = 2 already needs 156. Larger chunks buy context per chunk but spend the budget faster.
Simplified: we count words as tokens. Real tokenizers split words into subword tokens, so measure with the model's own tokenizer when you set a budget.

blocks.md: Getting the evidence into the window is not the end. Liu et al. (2023), *Lost in the Middle*, gave models 10, 20 or 30 retrieved Wikipedia passages where exactly one held the answer, and moved that passage through every position. Performance was highest when the answer was at the start or end and dropped in the middle, including for models sold as long-context. Their open-domain case study found readers saturate long before retriever recall: going from 20 to 50 retrieved documents improved accuracy only about 1.5% for GPT-3.5-Turbo and about 1% for Claude-1.3.

blocks.title: Lost in the middle: accuracy by position of the answer

scenes.caption: GPT-3.5-Turbo answering Natural Questions with 20 documents in the prompt, exactly one of which holds the answer. With the answer first, accuracy is 75.8%.
Move the same document toward the middle and accuracy falls to 53.8% at position 10, then recovers to 63.2% at the end. The curve is U-shaped.
With no documents at all the model scores 56.1%. In the middle positions the retrieved context made it worse than closed-book.

blocks.md:
A cheap mitigation that follows from this finding: put the strongest chunks at the edges of the context. Alternate the ranked list between the front and the back, so rank 1 goes first, rank 2 last, rank 3 second, and so on. For our five B chunks the order becomes D1.1, D1.5, D1.2, D1.3, D6.2, and the weakest of the five, D1.2, sits in the middle.

Notice the catch: this ordering trusts the retriever's ranks, and our retriever put the 6 weeks chunk (D1.3) at rank 4. Better ranking, from a reranker or contextual chunks, helps both what is retrieved and where it lands.

Three separate decisions shape the context: **how many** chunks (top-k), **how many tokens** they may use (the budget, set by the window minus everything else), and **in what order** they appear. Tune them together; raising k without a budget or an ordering rule mostly adds noise to the middle.

blocks.question: You raise k from 20 to 50 on a long-context model and recall@k rises from 80% to 90%, but end-to-end accuracy barely moves. Which explanation does Liu et al.'s case study support?
options: The retriever is broken, because recall should not rise with k
The reader saturates: it fails to use the extra, mostly mid-context documents, while cost and latency grow
Long-context models ignore everything after the first 20 documents by design
Accuracy can never exceed recall@20
blocks.explain: Liu et al. saw exactly this: reader accuracy saturated long before retriever recall did, with roughly 1% to 1.5% gain from 20 to 50 documents. More evidence in the window is not the same as evidence the model uses.

blocks.question: With the toy budget of 60 words, a teammate proposes Strategy A with k = 3 because D1 ranks first and contains both facts. What goes wrong?
options: Nothing; 3 whole documents fit in 60 words
D1 is dropped because whole documents cannot be ranked
The three documents total 93 words, so D6 and D2 do not fit; fill-in-rank-order keeps D1 alone, which happens to be enough here but leaves no room for a second source
The answer reserve grows automatically to fit
blocks.explain: D1 (44) + D6 (24) + D2 (25) = 93 words, over the 60-word context budget. Whole-document chunks spend the budget fast; here D1 alone holds both facts, but for any question needing two documents this strategy fails.

lessons.title: Prompting the generator to answer with citations

blocks.md: The prompt is where retrieval hands off to generation. A RAG prompt usually has three parts: **instructions** (use only the sources, cite them, say when the answer is missing), the **sources**, numbered and labeled with where they came from, and the **question**. Numbering is what makes citations possible: the model can write [1] and a program can map [1] back to a document and chunk.

blocks.code:
SYSTEM:
Answer the question using only the numbered sources below.
Cite sources like [1] after each sentence. If the sources do not
contain the answer, say you do not know.

[1] (D1 Parental leave) Northwind gives paid parental leave to every
full-time employee. The primary caregiver receives 16 weeks. A secondary
caregiver receives 6 weeks. Leave must begin within 12 months of the
birth or adoption. Send leave requests to the People team, who approve them.
[2] (D6 Benefits overview) Northwind benefits include health insurance,
retirement matching, parental leave, vacation and sick leave. ...
[3] (D2 Vacation) Full-time employees earn 20 vacation days per year.
Up to 5 unused days carry over. Your manager must approve vacation
requests two weeks ahead.

USER:
How long is parental leave for a secondary caregiver, and who approves
the leave request?
blocks.caption: The Strategy A top-3 context packed into a citation prompt (D6 truncated here for space). This ignores the toy 128-word window from the previous lesson, which would keep D1 alone; assume a larger window from here on.

blocks.md:
Barnett et al. report a related lesson from one of their case studies: adding the file name and chunk number to the retrieved context helped the reader extract the required information. Labels are cheap and they help both the model and the person checking the answer.

The abstain instruction targets the case where retrieval finds nothing useful. Without it, a model asked about content that is not in the corpus can be fooled into answering anyway.

How do you know if citations are any good? **ALCE** (Gao et al., 2023) is a benchmark that makes systems retrieve passages and write answers with citations, and scores citation quality automatically with an NLI model (TRUE, a T5-11B model fine-tuned on natural language inference) that decides whether a premise entails a statement.

- **Citation recall** (per statement): 1 if the statement has at least one citation and the concatenation of its cited passages entails it, else 0.
- **Citation precision** (per citation): a citation scores 1 only if its statement has citation recall 1 and the citation is not irrelevant. It is irrelevant if it does not support the statement alone *and* the remaining citations still support the statement without it.

Suppose the model, given the prompt above, answers:

*A secondary caregiver gets 6 weeks of paid parental leave [1][2]. Your manager approves the leave request [3]. Leave must begin within 12 months of the birth or adoption [1].*

The second sentence is wrong for this company. The model blended in the vacation rule from D2, a distractor that retrieval placed in the context.

blocks.title: Which sources each answer sentence cites and is supported by

scenes.caption: What the model cited (1 = cited). s1 cites [1][2], s2 cites [3], s3 cites [1]. Four citations in total.
What each source actually entails (1 = supports the sentence on its own). Only D1 supports s1 and s3. Nothing supports s2: D2 is about vacation requests, and D1 names the People team.
Compare the two grids. Citation [2] on s1 adds no support (irrelevant), and citation [3] on s2 supports nothing, so s2 fails citation recall.

blocks.caption: s1 and s3 are supported by their citations, s2 is not. Of four citations, [1] on s1 and [1] on s3 score 1; [2] on s1 is irrelevant, and [3] on s2 scores 0 because s2 has citation recall 0.

blocks.md: A citation is a claim, not a proof. The model can attach [3] to a sentence [3] does not support, as it did here. ALCE found even the best models lacked complete citation support about 50% of the time on ELI5, so check citations automatically rather than trusting their presence.

ALCE also compared ways of getting citations. Simply putting retrieved passages in context and asking for citations (their VANILLA setup) came close to the best of the prompting strategies they tried. Answering closed-book and then attaching the best-matching passage afterwards (POSTCITE) gave much worse citation quality: its citation recall on ASQA was 47% lower than VANILLA's. Citations work best when the evidence is in the context while the answer is written.

blocks.question: A statement cites [2][5]. Passage [5] alone entails it; [2] alone does not, and [5] without [2] still entails it. How does ALCE score this?
options: Citation recall 1; citation [2] counts as irrelevant, lowering precision
Citation recall 0, because [2] does not support the statement
Citation recall 1 and precision 1, since the statement is supported
Citation recall 0.5, one supporting passage out of two
blocks.explain: Recall asks whether the concatenation of cited passages entails the statement: yes, thanks to [5]. Precision checks each citation: [2] neither supports alone nor is needed with the others, so it is irrelevant.

blocks.question: Which prompt change most directly reduces confident answers to questions the corpus cannot answer?
options: Raising the sampling temperature
Moving the question before the sources
Asking for longer answers
Instructing the model to say it does not know when the sources lack the answer
blocks.explain: Barnett et al.'s first failure point is a question the documents cannot answer, where the system should say it does not know but can be fooled into answering. An explicit abstain instruction is the first defense; checking it needs test questions whose answer is absent.

blocks.md:
End-to-end accuracy tells you that an answer is wrong, not why. A wrong answer can come from the retriever (the fact never reached the prompt) or from the generator (the fact was there and the model ignored or garbled it), and the fixes are completely different. So evaluate the two halves separately.

**Ragas** (Es et al., 2023) proposed metrics computed by prompting an LLM, without human-written reference answers, for three dimensions: faithfulness, answer relevance and context relevance. The Ragas library has since added reference-based retrieval metrics, context precision and context recall.

blocks.caption: Faithfulness: an LLM splits the answer into short statements S, then checks each against the retrieved context. V is the set it judges supported.

blocks.md:
Apply it to our answer from lesson 4. Statements: (s1) a secondary caregiver gets 6 weeks of paid parental leave, supported by D1; (s2) your manager approves the leave request, not supported; (s3) leave must begin within 12 months, supported by D1. So $F = 2/3 \approx 0.67$. In this toy the judgments are made by hand to stand in for the LLM judge.

**Answer relevance** asks whether the answer addresses the question, ignoring truth. Ragas has an LLM generate $n$ questions from the answer, embeds them, and averages their cosine similarity with the real question; incomplete or padded answers score lower.

blocks.tex: \text{Context Precision@}K = \frac{\sum_{k=1}^{K} \text{Precision@}k \cdot v_k}{\text{relevant items in top } K} \qquad \text{Context Recall} = \frac{\text{reference claims supported by context}}{\text{reference claims}}
blocks.caption: As defined in the Ragas docs. v_k is 1 if the chunk at rank k is relevant. Precision rewards relevant chunks ranked early; recall checks the reference answer's claims against the retrieved context.

blocks.md: For the toy, the reference answer has two claims: (c1) 6 weeks for a secondary caregiver, (c2) the People team approves. A chunk is relevant if it contains either claim.

blocks.title: Retrieval metrics for three toy contexts

scenes.caption: Strategy A top-3 (D1, D6, D2): relevance flags 1, 0, 0. The relevant chunk is at rank 1, so context precision is 1.0, and D1 holds both reference claims, so context recall is 1.0.
Strategy B top-3 (D1.1, D6.2, D1.5): flags 0, 0, 1. Precision@3 is 1/3, so context precision is 0.333. Only the People team claim is covered, so recall is 0.5.
Strategy B top-5 adds D1.3 and D1.2: flags 0, 0, 1, 1, 0. Context precision is (1/3 + 2/4) / 2 = 0.417 and recall reaches 1.0.

blocks.md:
Now put the two halves side by side.

- **Strategy A**: context recall 1.0 but faithfulness 0.67. The facts were all retrieved and the generator still went wrong, misled by distractor D2. Fix the **generation** side: tighter context, a stronger instruction, or a better model.
- **Strategy B, k = 3**: context recall 0.5. No generator can produce 6 weeks from this context without using its own memory. Fix the **retrieval** side: larger k, better ranking, contextual chunks.

blocks.prompt: With Strategy B top-3, the model answers "6 weeks, approved by the People team", which is fully correct. What is its faithfulness score against the retrieved context?
blocks.reveal: **0.5.** The 6 weeks statement is not in D1.1, D6.2 or D1.5, so it is unsupported even though it is true. Faithfulness measures grounding in the context, not truth. A correct but unfaithful answer came from the model's own memory, which is exactly what RAG is supposed to replace, and it is unverifiable for the user.

blocks.md: Read the metrics as a grid. Low context recall: a **retrieval** problem. High context recall but low faithfulness: a **generation** problem. High faithfulness but wrong answer: the context itself was wrong or stale, an **index** problem.

LLM judges are themselves models. On the WikiEval dataset, Ragas agreed with human annotators 95% of the time on faithfulness, 78% on answer relevance and 70% on context relevance. Spot-check the judge on your data, and note that context precision as computed here treats a 44-word chunk and a 12-word chunk the same, so it does not see how much noise a big chunk brings.

blocks.question: Your RAG chatbot gives wrong answers on 20% of test questions. On those, context recall averages 0.95 and faithfulness 0.55. Where should you work first?
options: The chunker: chunks are too small
Top-k: retrieve more chunks
The generation side: the right facts are in context but the answers make unsupported claims
The embedding model: retrieval is missing facts
blocks.explain: Context recall near 1 says the evidence is reaching the prompt. Faithfulness of 0.55 says nearly half the statements are not supported by it. That points at the prompt, the context noise, or the model, not at retrieval.

blocks.question: Why is faithfulness alone not enough to evaluate a RAG system?
options: It needs a human-written reference answer
An answer can be fully faithful to retrieved context that is wrong, stale or irrelevant, and can say I do not know faithfully
It only works for single-sentence answers
It rewards answers that cite many sources
blocks.explain: Faithfulness compares the answer to the context, not to the truth or to the question. Pair it with answer relevance and with retrieval metrics. Ragas faithfulness needs no reference answer, which is part of its appeal.

lessons.title: The seven failure points and how to debug them

blocks.md: Barnett et al. (2024) built three RAG systems in research, education and biomedical question answering (the last on the BioASQ dataset, 4017 documents and 1000 questions) and catalogued where they broke. They call the result **seven failure points** (FP). Each maps to a stage of the pipeline you have now built piece by piece.

blocks.title: Where the seven failure points occur

scenes.caption: The query path from Barnett et al., simplified to five stages. Each failure point is a place where the needed information is lost or mishandled.
FP1 Missing Content: the answer is not in the corpus at all. The right behavior is I do not know; the danger is a plausible invented answer.
FP2 Missed the Top Ranked Documents: the answer is in the corpus but ranks below the top-K cut. Our B top-3 case: D1.3 at rank 4.
FP3 Not in Context: the document was retrieved but dropped while consolidating results into the prompt, for example by a token budget or chunk cap.
FP4 to FP7 happen in the reader even with the answer in context: not extracted, wrong format, incorrect specificity, incomplete. Our manager approves error is FP4.

blocks.md:
The full list, in the paper's words where possible:

1. **Missing Content**: the question cannot be answered from the available documents.
2. **Missed the Top Ranked Documents**: the answer is in a document that did not rank highly enough to be returned in the top K.
3. **Not in Context**: documents with the answer were retrieved but did not make it into the context, typically when many documents are returned and consolidated.
4. **Not Extracted**: the answer is in the context but the LLM failed to extract it, typically due to noise or contradicting information.
5. **Wrong Format**: the LLM ignored a format instruction such as a table or list.
6. **Incorrect Specificity**: the answer is too general or too specific for the user's need.
7. **Incomplete**: the answer misses information that was in the context.

Our toy produced four of them:

- **FP1**: ask Northwind's system about bereavement leave. No document covers it, so the only correct answer is I do not know.
- **FP2**: Strategy B with k = 3 ranks the 6 weeks chunk 4th.
- **FP3**: Strategy B retrieves top-5, but a builder that caps the prompt at 3 chunks drops D1.3 again, now after retrieval succeeded.
- **FP4**: Strategy A puts both facts in context, yet the vacation rule in D2 leads the model to say your manager approves.

Two takeaways from the paper matter more than the list. First, validation of a RAG system is only feasible during operation: real users ask questions you did not predict, so log queries, retrieved chunk ids and answers, and evaluate them. Second, robustness evolves rather than being designed in at the start: chunk size, embedding strategy, retrieval strategy, consolidation strategy, context size and prompts all need calibrating against those logs.

Debug in pipeline order. For a bad answer, check: is the fact in the corpus (FP1)? In the top-K (FP2)? In the final prompt (FP3)? Only if all three are yes is it a generation failure (FP4 to FP7). Logging the chunk ids at each stage makes this a lookup instead of a guess.

blocks.question: A user asks for the refund policy as a bulleted list. The answer is correct and grounded but comes back as one paragraph. Which failure point is this?
options: FP5 Wrong Format
FP4 Not Extracted
FP7 Incomplete
FP2 Missed the Top Ranked Documents
blocks.explain: The facts are present and right; only the requested format was ignored. Barnett et al. define FP5 as the LLM ignoring an instruction to extract information in a certain format such as a table or list.

blocks.question: Logs show the correct chunk at rank 2 from the retriever, but it never appears in the final prompt because the prompt builder deduplicates by document and keeps only the first chunk per document. Which failure point is this?
options: FP2 Missed the Top Ranked Documents
FP3 Not in Context
FP4 Not Extracted
FP1 Missing Content
blocks.explain: Retrieval succeeded: the chunk ranked 2nd. It was lost during consolidation into the context, which is FP3. Raising k would not help; the consolidation rule has to change.

blocks.question: Asked "What are the key points in policies D1, D3 and D5?", the system summarizes D1 well and mentions D3 and D5 in one line each, although all three were in context. Which failure point fits, and what do Barnett et al. suggest?
options: FP6 Incorrect Specificity; retrieve fewer chunks
FP1 Missing Content; add documents
FP3 Not in Context; raise the token budget
FP7 Incomplete; ask such questions separately, one per document
blocks.explain: The information was in the context and available, yet the answer missed some of it: that is FP7. The paper's own example is a question about documents A, B and C, and it suggests asking those separately.
